extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato, classical philosophy, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Critical commentary and analytic criteria for reading Plato's Gorgias: evaluates argument forms, moral/ethical claims, rhetorical practice, and the dialogue's aims and metaphors. Intended to guide close reading and judgement of the dialogue's strengths and weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and precision of definitions / presence of formal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal logic has as yet no existence; the old difficulty of framing a definition recurs. The ambiguity of several words, such as nature, custom, the honourable, the good, is not cleared up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether key terms are defined clearly and used consistently. Note places where ambiguity undermines argument; lack of formal logical structure should be flagged as a defect when it causes equivocation or misleading inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of fallacious antitheses and false oppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantages which Socrates gains over Polus are due to a false antithesis of pleasure and good, and to an erroneous assertion that an agent and a patient may be described by similar predicates. Nothing can be more fallacious than the contradiction which he pretends to have discovered in the answers of Gorgias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for improperly constructed oppositions or pairings (e.g., pleasure vs good) and for arguments that rely on misleading contrasts. Mark instances where the dialectic depends on a false dichotomy or equivocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between reality and appearance (real vs seeming)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sophists are still floundering about the distinction of the real and seeming. Figures of speech are made the basis of arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether speakers conflate appearance and reality. Identify rhetorical or figurative moves presented as literal proof, and judge their validity for establishing truth rather than persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and ironic character of the dialectic
rubrics_metrics.description: Having regard to the age of Plato and the ironical character of his writings ... Socrates often a sort of dialectical fiction, by which he conducts himself and others to his own ideal of life and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether Socratic questioning is genuine inquiry or a pedagogical/ironic device steering interlocutors. Determine how this affects the plausibility and charitable reading of the opponents' positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness and limits of analogies (arts/virtues; disease/justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The illusive analogy of the arts and the virtues also continues. The analogy of disease and injustice, or of medicine and justice, is certainly imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate analogies for scope and applicability; point out overextended metaphors and where analogy is partial and misleading. Distinguish suggestive figures from arguments treated as literal equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures and metaphors vs. treating them as realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato sometimes reasons from them [figures of speech] as if they were not figures but realities, due to the defective logical analysis of his age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag passages where metaphorical language is used to support literal claims. Recommend reinterpreting such passages as illustrative rather than deductive unless explicit justification is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and coherence of ethical concepts (pleasure, good, courage, knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure and good are not the same; knowledge and courage are not the same either with pleasure or good, or with one another. Socrates' division of empirical habits, shams, flatteries, and arts concerned with higher interests is central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test internal consistency: are ethical categories clearly distinct and applied uniformly? Note contradictions or unstable shifts in meaning across the dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of punishment: vindictive vs corrective purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s theory of punishment is partly vindictive, partly corrective. Most men are not incurable, and their punishment is intended for their improvement. He does not distinguish between suffering which improves and suffering which only punishes and deters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the dialogue's moral doctrine, ask whether punishment is justified as corrective (therapeutic) or retributive, and whether Plato explains mechanisms by which punishment effects moral improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealizing suffering and its justificatory role
rubrics_metrics.description: The idealizing of suffering is one of the conceptions which have exercised the greatest influence; Plato is convinced that somehow such an one must be happy in life or after death. He supposes a day of retribution and frames life with a view to this unknown future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the extent to which the text relies on idealizing suffering (martyrdom, noble death) to justify ethical claims. Consider whether ethical conclusions depend on belief in posthumous rewards/punishments and how that affects their persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial purpose: identifying the dialogue's central aim
rubrics_metrics.description: The main purpose of the Gorgias is not to answer questions about a future world, but to place in antagonism the true and false life, and to contrast the judgments and opinions of men with judgment according to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orient interpretation around the dialogue's primary aim: assess passages for how they serve the central contrast (true vs false life) rather than peripheral theological or metaphysical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of political/ethical scope (agent-centered vs concern for others)
rubrics_metrics.description: He [Plato] is thought to have erred in 'considering the agent only, and making no reference to the happiness of others, as affected by him.' Yet the duty of imparting truth and the social principle are present; in ancients ethics and politics are merged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the dialogue's ethics sufficiently accounts for the effects on others. Note tensions between a primarily agent-focused ideal and broader social or political obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical vs. genuine oratory: flattery compared to true statesmanlike oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two species of oratory; one a flattery, another which has a real regard for the citizens. The true orator desires to implant justice and eradicate injustice and is like a physician for the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate rhetorical techniques aimed at pleasing the audience from rhetoric aimed at moral improvement. Evaluate speakers by their end (flattery vs cultivation of virtue) and by evidence of consistent life-long design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of historical statesmen by moral improvement of citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The statesman’s proper business is to make the citizens as good as possible. We must ask whom he has made better; Pericles and others may have constructed docks and harbours but did not improve character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political figures or policies in the text, prioritize measures of moral and civic improvement over material or administrative achievements. Ask for concrete evidence that leaders foster virtue in citizens.
